frames.heading: Primes look random
frames.say: A prime divides only by 1 and itself. They follow **no obvious pattern**.

frames.heading: So count them instead
frames.say: Climb one step at each prime. The staircase is **surprisingly regular**.
frames.caption: Height: how many primes you have passed.

frames.heading: A smooth curve comes close
frames.say: Gauss found a formula that **tracks the staircase**. It is close, never exact.
frames.caption: The question becomes: how big can the gap get?

frames.heading: Riemann found the key
frames.say: His zeta function equals zero at special points. The ones that matter sit in **one narrow strip**.
frames.caption: Each dot is a zero, in the complex plane. These are the first twelve with positive height.

frames.heading: Each zero adds a wave
frames.say: Add the waves and the smooth curve **bends into the staircase**. Try it.

big.label: zeros are enough to see the steps

frames.caption: This staircase weights each prime power by a logarithm, which makes the formula exact with all zeros.

frames.heading: The hypothesis
frames.say: Every zero that matters lies **exactly on the line ½**. Then the primes are as evenly spread as they can be.
frames.caption: One zero off the line would mean larger errors in the prime count.

frames.heading: Proved by machine, not yet understood
frames.say: A proof found with AI appeared on **20 November 2026**. Computers accept it; **people cannot read it yet**.

rows.t: A proof by Levent Alpöge of Anthropic, with Claude
rows.sub: 20 November 2026, as Lean code and a four-page note.

rows.t: Lean's maintainers certify the statement and the proof
rows.sub: 21 November. Several independent checkers accept it; one long rerun is unfinished.

rows.t: A proof people can read, and peer review
rows.sub: The Clay prize also needs publication and time.
